concepts.name: Kinetic friction
concepts.statement: When two surfaces in contact are moving relative to one another, the friction between them is called kinetic friction. It is the force that slows a hockey puck sliding on ice, and it is the one that behaves simply enough to be written as a single product.

concepts.name: Static friction
concepts.statement: When the surfaces are not moving relative to one another, static friction can act between them. It is a responsive force, growing to be equal and opposite to whatever you push with, up to a limit, which is why a heavy crate can be pushed harder and harder and still not move.

concepts.name: Coefficient of friction
concepts.statement: The coefficient of friction is the number that carries what the two materials are. It has no units, its magnitude is usually between 0 and 1.0, and for the same pair of surfaces the kinetic coefficient is smaller than the static one, which is why a crate is easier to keep moving than it was to start.

concepts.name: Magnitude of static friction, $\kfs \le \mu_{\text{s}}\kN$
concepts.statement: Static friction can take any magnitude from zero up to a maximum, and the maximum is the coefficient of static friction times the normal force. The friction is whatever it needs to be to keep the surfaces at rest, until the applied force passes that maximum and the object moves.

concepts.name: Magnitude of kinetic friction, $\kfk = \mu_{\text{k}}\kN$
concepts.statement: Once an object is moving, the friction on it is the coefficient of kinetic friction times the normal force. Friction that obeys this rule is said to behave simply, and its magnitude does not depend on the area in contact or, to a good approximation, on the speed.

concepts.name: Friction on a slope, $\kfk = \mu_{\text{k}} m\kg\cos\theta$
concepts.statement: On a slope, the normal force is not the whole weight but only its component perpendicular to the surface, so the kinetic friction is the coefficient times mg cos θ. An object that slides down the slope at constant speed therefore has a coefficient of kinetic friction equal to tan θ.

concepts.name: The atomic origin of friction
concepts.statement: Friction is proportional to the normal force but not to the total area in contact, and that is only explained by looking at the surfaces closely: they touch at their high spots, the actual area of contact grows as they are pressed together, and they warm because the rubbing sets their atomic lattices vibrating.

concepts.name: Drag force, $\kFD = \tfrac{1}{2}C\rho A\kv^2$
concepts.statement: For a large object that is not moving too slowly, the drag force is proportional to the square of the speed, and the constant in front gathers the drag coefficient, the area facing the fluid and the density of the fluid. Doubling the speed of a car therefore multiplies the drag on it by about four.

concepts.name: Drag coefficient
concepts.statement: The drag coefficient is the dimensionless number that carries the shape of the object. It is determined empirically, usually in a wind tunnel, and it is why aerodynamic shaping matters: a Toyota Camry has a coefficient of 0.28 and a Hummer H2 one of 0.64, and a skydiver's own coefficient changes with the position they fall in.

concepts.name: Terminal velocity
concepts.statement: A falling body speeds up until the drag force has grown equal to its weight. The net force is then zero, so by Newton's second law the acceleration is zero and the speed stays where it is. Terminal velocity is what free fall becomes once the air is no longer neglected.

concepts.name: Terminal velocity, $\kvt = \sqrt{2m\kg/\rho C A}$
concepts.statement: Setting the drag force equal to the weight and solving for the speed gives the terminal velocity in terms of the mass, the drag coefficient, the area facing the fluid and the density of the fluid. It is why a 75 kg skydiver falls at about 350 km/h head first and at about 200 km/h spread eagle.

concepts.name: Stokes' law, $\kFs = 6\pi r\eta\kv$
concepts.statement: When the object is very small, is going very slowly, or is in a medium denser than air, the drag is proportional to the speed itself rather than to its square, and the force is 6πrηv. This is the drag that a bacterium, a grain of pollen or a dust particle feels.

concepts.name: Size and terminal velocity
concepts.statement: Divide an animal's length, breadth and height each by ten and its weight falls to a thousandth while its surface falls only to a hundredth, so the smaller animal meets relatively ten times the resistance. That is why a squirrel can fall from a tree and walk away and a person cannot.

concepts.name: Deformation
concepts.statement: A change in shape due to the application of a force is a deformation. Even very small forces are known to cause some deformation, and for small ones two things are observed: the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed, and the size of the deformation is proportional to the force.

concepts.name: The elastic region, permanent deformation and tensile strength
concepts.statement: The proportionality between force and deformation holds only so far. Past the straight part of the graph the deformation is still elastic, past that the object is permanently deformed, and at the tensile strength it fractures. Bones are brittle, so their elastic region is small and the fracture abrupt.

concepts.name: Change in length, $\kdL = \frac{1}{\kY}\frac{\kF}{A}\kLo$
concepts.statement: The change in length of a wire or rod is proportional to the force and to the original length and inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area, and the constant that carries the substance is Young's modulus. A long guitar string stretches more than a short one, and a thick one stretches less than a thin one.

concepts.name: Stress
concepts.statement: The ratio of force to area is defined as stress, measured in newtons per square meter. Writing the force in this way is what lets one number describe a material rather than one particular rod, since the same force on a thinner wire is a larger stress.

concepts.name: Strain
concepts.statement: The ratio of the change in length to the original length is defined as strain, and it is a unitless quantity. Most materials behave elastically while the strain is less than about 0.1%, and a support tendon such as the ones in your leg can change its length by as much as ten percent.

concepts.name: Stress and strain, $\text{stress} = \kY \times \text{strain}$
concepts.statement: Rearranged, the equation for the change in length says that the stress is Young's modulus times the strain. In this form it is Hooke's law again, with stress in place of force and strain in place of deformation, which is why one shape of statement covers a stretched wire, a sheared bookcase and a compressed cube.

concepts.name: Shear deformation, $\kdx = \frac{1}{\kS}\frac{\kF}{A}\kLo$
concepts.statement: A force applied perpendicular to the length and parallel to the cross-sectional area shears the object sideways, and the constant is the shear modulus. The equation is logical: it is easier to bend a long thin pencil than a short thick one, and both bend more easily than a steel rod of the same size.

concepts.name: Change in volume, $\Delta V = \frac{1}{\kBb}\frac{\kF}{A}V_0$
concepts.statement: An object squeezed evenly on all its surfaces changes its volume rather than its length, and the constant is the bulk modulus. Gases compress easily because their molecules are far apart, while liquids and solids are extraordinarily difficult to compress, which is why seawater five kilometers down has lost only 2.3% of its volume.

concepts.name: Tensile strength
concepts.statement: The tensile strength of a material is the breaking stress, the stress that will cause permanent deformation or fracture of the material.
